notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1321.tmp1321.opp-lat: Paragraph 2 of the letter: 'vestra solertia devota' does not construe easily with 'Fausti ... praedecessoris'; I read it as 'solertia devota ... praedecessoris vestri', i.e. Faustus's diligence, not Urbicus's. 'delicium' read as 'delictum' (fault), which the contrast with 'mercedis praemium' requires; as printed it would mean 'your delight'. 'silente peplo' read as 'silentii peplo' (cloak of silence). 'populo diffuso' is obscure: taken as 'spread abroad before the people'. Section 1: 'pondere' seems corrupt, perhaps for 'ponderare' (to weigh) or a form of 'prodere' (to set forth); rendered 'to weigh'. Section 3: 'ingenii' read as 'ingenti' (huge). Section 4: 'imperavit' read as 'superavit' (overcame). Section 5: 'praesint' read as 'praestet' (grants); 'cumque' read as 'eumque'. Whether 'moles' is a place name or a common noun (a mole or breakwater) is uncertain. Section 6: 'preces malignas' read as 'preces malignus'. Decomeco is left as printed; its form and location are unconfirmed. Albinus is given as printed; he may be the saint otherwise known as Alban.

Several evident scanning errors read as intended: in 7 'eum' as 'cum'; in 8 'orbis' as 'urbis', 'suos' as 'suus', 'implorate' as 'implorare'; in 9 'fugietis' as 'fugiens'; in 10 'redivivos' as 'redivivus'; in 11 'indictum' as 'inflictum'; in 12 'praestate' as 'praestare'. In 12 'Teucros' makes no sense and is read as 'teneros' ('tender'). In 10 the subject of 'could not rise' is taken to be the son. In 13 'vehiculi' (vehicle) is taken as the bier carrying his body. Quinto Kalendas Decembris = 27 November.

Scanning errors corrected: 'mullis' (multis), 'bominibus' (hominibus), 'cbaritatis' (caritatis), 'commixtemque' (read as commixtoque). In 15, 'jugi oblatione' is obscure; rendered as 'continual pressing' (the apostles' repeated offering of the honour). 'Ad complendam eam sancto Maximo orationem' may also mean the apostles deferred to each other in offering Maximus the completion of the prayer. In 16, 'is cui praesens celebramus officium' could refer to God or to the saint; the antecedent is unclear.

nodes.text: THE LIFE OF SAINT MAXIMUS BY SAINT DYNAMIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AND PATRICIAN. (Surius, Acts of the Saints, vol. II.) Dedicatory letter.
To the lord and most blessed Father, *papa* [a title of honour for a bishop] Urbicus, Dynamius the Patrician [sends] greetings.

Father, since, kindled with the ardour of apostolic faith, you search with careful inquiry into everything concerning the miracles of Saint Maximus that a faithful account of his deeds makes known, you do not cease to press my lack of skill; and with fatherly admonitions you also affirm, with the authority of a preacher, that I shall be made guilty in no small measure of the harm of that offence unless I take care to add to his Life, which, as is well established, I wrote some years ago in rustic speech, everything that you have evidently now discovered about his wonders. For this reason I am confounded by a double shame, since neither is the ability to speak granted to me, nor is the safety of silence allowed. If I speak, my exposed rusticity shows an unskilled mind. For if it had been permitted, I could at least have pleased by concise expression, since no increase of learning can come to my aid. Placed, then, between these two difficulties, I have resolved to obey your commands, intending to please by obedience, not by learning. You have told me, then, that you have turned over old volumes of papers, into which the devoted diligence of the most blessed bishop Faustus, your predecessor, had gathered something of his works, from which you could scarcely make out a few things, by inference rather than by sight. For the devouring power of envious age had consumed very many of the things that lay hidden there. And you judged that it would be quite impious if these few out of many were not handed on to eternal memory through the sequence of my writings. Therefore I consider that I have in part satisfied your wishes, since the reading, drawn out to a long extension, now follows in multiplied form. Whenever, once read, it causes weariness in its hearers, this can be laid to your fault; if it brings the prize of a reward, nothing from that will likewise belong to me, who, compelled by your commands, have written at greater length than I wished, and have given up the refuge of brevity. Since, then, most prudent shepherd, you strip me of the cloak of silence and lay me bare of the covering of taciturnity, I beg you to protect me, now that I am spread abroad before the whole people, with the defence of your intercession. Whenever the length of the reading is gone through again, may the unpolished diction not displease, since the course of the holy narrative commends it. For there is no doubt that, as much as you set forth with the whole devotion of your heart the deeds of that holy bishop, so much you strive in your works to follow, with the whole eagerness of your mind, in the footsteps of him whose adorning deeds you love: so long as, by divine favour and his patronage, there may be granted to you a long tranquillity of temporal life and the ability you desire for holy work, my truly holy lord and most blessed *papa*.
HERE BEGINS THE LIFE.

1. Today is celebrated the day of the holy solemnity of the most blessed Maximus, bishop of the city of Riez, which is renewed every year through the reviving channels of time; and pious devotion of mind admonishes us, and ancient custom compels us, to weigh his deeds. For unless things that have been ascertained as clear and in no way doubtful through the testimony of others are set down in written records, what was done in ancient times is often reported in varying ways by new authors. And so, that the distinctions of his mystical activity may contain nothing ambiguous, and that popular affection may make none of them fabulous or suspect of falsehood, the things done and proved by him must be narrated in truthful speech. Yet of these very things, lest excessive length bring weariness to the hearer, we have passed over a great many in silence and recorded a few.

2. The blessed Maximus took the beginning of life on his own estate, whose name is Decomeco, born of Christian parents and at once made a Christian. From the very first stages of infancy, ever growing in lofty humility, he so disciplined the tender years of his age with maturity of character that by the grace of holiness he claimed for himself the proper meaning of his name. And after he had passed out of boyhood, he tamed the enticements and blandishments of wantonness by the mastery and stern judgement of his mind, in order that he might obtain the palm of unspoiled purity in the virginity he had promised, and might triumph in the heavenly kingdoms with the flesh sent under the yoke. He was indeed endowed with the adornments of all good qualities, and rightly deserves to be exalted with praise and proclamation: for he was venerable in countenance, gentle in appearance, placid in expression, serene in spirit, strong in patience, conspicuous for magnanimity, a lover of peace, generous toward enemies, disdainful of things that pass away, burning with desire for heavenly things, weighing eternal things against temporal, and holding temporal things cheap and despising them in favour of eternal. And in order that he might know the precepts of the divine law more inwardly, he made such progress in letters by the natural sharpness of his intellect that in his eagerness for reading he sought food for his soul, and like the bees drew the nectar of eternal sweetness. And although he crushed all the kindling of carnal vices, and shone on every side with his excellent way of life, he nonetheless broke the strength of his body by constant abstinence, pursuing and restraining the vices of the flesh before they were born, so that for martyrdom he seems to have lacked only an executioner. For beyond doubt he made himself a martyr, both in torment and in merit.

3. Moreover, abandoning also the whole abundance of his means, he made for the monastery of Lérins, where as a just man he might find everlasting riches: following the precepts of the Gospel, knowing that he could not become perfect unless he sold all that he had and made himself a stranger to all wealth. In that community, since he loved everyone with perfect charity, he was likewise loved by all. And such fervour appeared in him that, before he had embraced the monastic rule of living or its mystical institutions, he already seemed outstanding in his way of life, and afterwards he both succeeded in office and was made equal in merits to Saint Honoratus, his predecessor, a man most richly adorned with the highest virtues, who had been abbot there. While in this office he was guarding the flock entrusted to him with pastoral diligence, and every night, while the others were taken up with sleep, was going round the monastery, it happened, contrary to custom, that a certain monk, still a boy, moved by some curiosity or concern, followed him. And behold, the devil, the plotter, presented himself to the sight of the most blessed man in a huge and terrifying form. But since he could not terrify the man clothed in spiritual armour, he struck the unsuspecting monk with such terror that, as he went back at once with trembling step to his cell, a most burning fever soon seized him.

4. Again that persistent impostor, hoping that he would somehow disturb the holy man, showed himself to him in the shape of a fiery dragon. But, terrified at once by the sign of the cross, he vanished. For the unconquered athlete no longer feared in the least an enemy so often overcome. And after he had travelled the whole circuit of the island of Lérins, he came quickly to the bed of the sick monk who, as we said, had fallen into a fever; and secretly at his side, pouring out prayers to God within the hidden places of his heart, he brought it about that the monk was soon restored to his former health, and the enemy, outwitted, was cheated of his prey. So a twofold power won an unconquered victory, when he both gave strength back to the sick man and overcame the adversary: the enemy lamenting the loss he had suffered, the monk rejoicing in the health he had recovered.

5. As this excellent shepherd was thus going round the Lord's sheepfold every night, lest anything adverse should happen, he came on one occasion to the shore of the sea which is called the Mole, and at once that old trickster dared by his illusions to set swiftly before his eyes what looked like a laden ship, and sailors busy at work in their usual way and gathering up the ship's tackle; and two of them came up to the blessed man's side, saying that they had arrived there for the sake of trade, since the outcome of the matter had shown that this would be not without enormous profit. They said they knew him as Maximus, the greatest no less in holiness than in name, and that in lands overseas he was so greatly desired by all that, if they could obtain him, they would hold nothing at a higher price. They would therefore make no greater gain than if they could put him aboard the ship and carry him off to Jerusalem, having found him, beyond expectation, by a happy success. And this would beyond doubt bring great honour and dignity to him, if he were brought by a fortunate voyage to the place where he was so eagerly awaited in the prayers of all. But the man of God, recognising the snare and evil trickery of the enemy, fortified himself with the sign of the holy cross, implored heavenly help, and then answered thus with spiritual authority: "The wickedness of a cheat and impostor cannot deceive the soldiers of Christ, nor can the malign one make sport with his frauds of those to whom God grants that they can foresee adverse things. And the prayers of the most blessed Honoratus have so fortified this island, after the dragon that inhabited it was driven out by him, that henceforth no way of doing harm lies open in it to the devil." At these words the sham ship vanished from the eyes of the man as he prayed, and he, returning at once to the oratory, urged the brothers to rise for vigils, and together with that holy community he paid the most solemn praises to him through whom he had won the victory over the enemy.

6. And as the fame of his outstanding miracles was flying through the whole world, by the zeal not only of the citizens but also of all the priests and bishops he was no less seized than elected for the bishopric of the city of Riez, and, though unwilling, was at once consecrated. And although, being already Maximus both in fact and in name, he scarcely seemed to have anything in which he could grow further, yet, that nothing might be lost to his name, just as he remained Maximus in work and deeds, so too he excelled in honour. Among the other adornments of right action, then, that shone in him, he was strong in patience, patient in benevolence, eager in freedom, abundant in liberality, beneficent in magnanimity, mild in humanity, diligent in application, sweet in charity, open to all in generosity, outstanding in teaching, singular in justice, lofty in humility, a despiser of riches, copious and overflowing in dignity. In the fortress of Riez he founded, with all the devotion of mind he could, a church in honour of the blessed Albinus, whose columns, which can be seen there even today, teams of oxen hauled to the place, yet in such a way that they felt no discomfort from so great a weight, his holiness bringing this about, so long as he was present as a tireless labourer on the building of the church. But if it happened that he was away, by the hidden contrivance of a most wicked demon all the oxen were so pressed down by their weight that they could be driven forward by no goads. Even if several others were yoked on, they all stayed unmoved, however savagely they were beaten and wounded. When a swift messenger reported this to the most blessed bishop, he came to the place without delay and with confidence, neither trembling with terror nor disturbed by grief. Then indeed the most wicked enemy could not deceive his eyes, nor withdraw himself from the sight of him, though he could not be seen by the eyes of all the people. And the holy man said to them: "You torment these beasts, which lack reason, in vain, since you cannot see the enemy's obstructions. But I see a little Ethiopian, throwing himself in the way of the oxen." Then on bended knees he prayed in supplication to God to turn aside the enemy's snares. That malign one, unable to bear his prayers, swiftly withdrew, not without a most foul stench. Soon, when the oxen that had been yoked on in addition were removed, the columns were hauled without any difficulty to the appointed place.

7. Nor have we thought we should leave out, for the strengthening of the Rhegians' faith, the following: when the most blessed bishop was bringing sacred relics with the greatest honour, singing psalms, to the basilica he had built, and they had come to the city gate, that verse unexpectedly came up in its order: "This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter by it." From this it can beyond doubt be concluded that that city has been so fortified by his prayers that, just as up to now, by Christ's favour, it has suffered no attacks of enemies over a long span of time, so henceforth too, with God's favour, it will by no means suffer them. For that outstanding shepherd, whom his deeds testify to be alive, could easily obtain from God after his death that the city of which he had been bishop should be fortified for all time by his illustrious merits, through the power of his body in the most holy church that he founded, which shines forth in the many benefits that are granted there to all.

8. Once, when the holy man was celebrating vigils in that same basilica with pastoral diligence, the nephew of Ansanus, deacon of Riez, that is, his brother's son, whom his parents had left as a small child when they departed this life, and whom he had taken in to bring up and loved more than if he had been his own son, was playing with some boys on the wall of that city, fell from the wall, broke his neck and died. Ansanus, greatly dismayed at the news of this, ran there quickly, snatched up the boy's body, covered it with garments, and carried it secretly to the blessed bishop, meanwhile considering within himself how he might lay it publicly at his feet and beg him in supplication to restore him to life. But because he knew that the most proven soldier of Christ shunned all boasting, he preferred to carry it to his chamber, lay it on his bed and cover it with his blankets, fully trusting that the spiritual physician could raise him by his prayers, since he was accustomed to bring health to the sick. From there, not indeed without much grief of mind, but yet full of confidence, he went to the bishop, who was keeping vigil in the church and standing in his place. On seeing him, the most merciful prelate, so that he might explain what had happened, ordered those singing psalms to be silent; and when the prayers had been completed with the usual devotion, he sharply rebuked the deacon Ansanus for what he had done. But he not only could not be driven off by threats, but, still more stricken in heart, threw himself at his feet and cried out that he would by no means let go of them unless he raised the dead boy, saying that he could do it very easily, since he had already learned, without anyone telling him, what had happened to the boy. Compelled by this persistence and constrained by reason, he wished to go privately with Ansanus to his bed; but he could not avoid the crowd of the people, who wished to be present at the miracle of so great a thing. So, after he came to the boy's lifeless little body, he began to implore divine help with his whole body, and taking the boy's hand with great confidence, he restored him to his former health. And all the people cried out: "Glory to you, God"; nor did any of them let himself be removed from there until he saw the boy moving and heard him speaking. Because of this tumult of the people he could scarcely be brought back to the vigils, even with the efforts of his clergy. In this miracle both the great faith of the deacon and the illustrious power of the bishop shone out.

9. Furthermore, it happened that a certain widow's only daughter, a young girl, departed this life; and when the wretched mother had laid her out on the bier to be carried out according to custom, she hurried in alarm to the blessed bishop and made known to him the cause of her grief by tears rather than words, begging that he pour out prayers over the lifeless body. The holy prelate, moved by compassion, could neither refuse nor delay this; but going to the corpse, with hands raised to heaven, he implored God prostrate, and the dead girl was restored to life. For at once, as if released from a heavy sleep, she awoke, opened her heavy eyes, and rose when called; her mother was filled with immense joy, all the people were astounded; the bishop, who by the merits of his miracles had loosed the rights of death, fleeing boasting, withdrew at once. But the people, praising God with loud voices, with a sort of civic violence tore apart and pulled to pieces the greater part of his garment, to keep it in place of relics; so that, to declare his miracles, what was barely left on his shoulders is preserved by the devotion of the faithful today.

10. A certain youth died choked by the bite of a rabid dog. The people saw it, went to the bishop, and begged him to come to the dead man. But he, held in doubtful thought, since on the one side he could not disregard the tears of the suppliants, and on the other he feared ostentation for himself, was at last overcome by compassion; he did what he was asked, came to the dead man, raised his hands to heaven, and likewise his streaming eyes, and with the people looking on he raised the dead man. His parents were there, beating their breasts with their fists, and so drenching their faces with tears over their son that he could not rise from the ground, though he was now alive again. Meanwhile, holding out one hand to his father and the other to his mother, he lifted up his tottering limbs as they raised him. The people cried out, "Thanks be to God"; he, restored to life, went back to his own lodging, he for whom a tomb was already being prepared; his parents exulted with incredible joy; they could scarcely believe their own eyes that the man who had been dead was alive. But behold, that dog which had mangled both this youth and many others with savage bites came into the bishop's sight; the bishop, roused, threw down his staff, raised his hands upward and prayed to the Lord, then at once breathed on the dog, and it was deprived of life. It hardly seems a wonder that the blessed bishop, wishing to protect the flock entrusted to him, destroyed its enemy with a deadly stroke, and that not with a sword or an armed hand, but with the breath of his mouth. Moreover, the wounds that dog had inflicted with its teeth on many of the common people the blessed bishop so healed by prayers and the sign of the cross that no trace of them appeared.

11. A wanton ox had wretchedly torn a man with its horn, so that his intestines poured out. Soon some people brought him to the bishop. Although in all his miracles he feared for himself lest he be assailed by pride of mind, he nevertheless received the man, so badly wounded, with mercy, warmed his entrails with hot compresses, handling them with his own hands, put them back in their place through the wound inflicted by the ox, gently bound up the wound itself with a sponge applied to it, and earnestly urged that no one but himself should dare to undo it. Then on the seventh day, taking off the bandages, he found the man so healthy that scarcely any sign of the wound seemed to be left.

12. The most holy man tamed the tender limbs of his body by the constant harshness of a hair shirt, which he used in place of an inner tunic; nor did he ever lay it aside, out of zeal for the cross, but even ordered that he be buried in it. He would never use baths, lest the constancy of mind with which, trampling on the delights and allurements of the flesh, he endured a martyrdom should grow soft. A certain blind man, condemned for fifteen years to perpetual darkness, continually begged the most holy man to restore sight to him by his prayers. But since the bishop put this off in order to avoid ostentation, the blind man asked Rusticus the subdeacon, who used to serve him, to lead him by night, when the bishop was visiting the churches, to the porch of the church from which he would come out. The subdeacon did this, and the blessed man, as he was going out of the church, gently bumped his feet against the blind man; the blind man embraced his venerable feet in supplication and begged him to restore his sight. So the bishop confidently besought the Lord, pressed the sign of the cross on his eyes, and the eyes long extinguished were soon restored. The bishop kissed the man and implored him to keep the matter silent to himself, which, however, he could not do for the immense exultation of his heart; although even if he had wished to conceal what had been done in secret, what was plainly seen by the eyes of all could not remain hidden.

13. Countless are the miracles of the most blessed bishop, and they cannot all be recounted, however long an account is woven. It was very easy for him to give light to the blind, to heal the lame, to raise the dead. In short, there was nothing he could not do, who had the Holy Spirit dwelling within him. Meanwhile, as he was renowned for so many miracles and immense mysteries, he learned the day of his death by divine revelation. Then, with the greatest humility, he publicly pressed everyone to allow him first to visit his native soil and his kinsfolk. Although this brought them great grief of mind, he nevertheless went off to his own people and foretold to them that his death was now imminent. So, having delighted them wonderfully by his arrival, he greatly troubled them with this most sorrowful news. And behold, as he laid himself on his bed as if to take sleep, amid the psalm-singing during the divine office, he breathed his last breath and happily passed to heaven on the fifth day before the Kalends of December; and then such an abundance of the sweetest fragrance arose for them as if all the flowers of springtime had been gathered into that place. Swift report of his death filled not only the city but the whole world. Crowds of the faithful from the peoples ran together from all sides, vying to touch even the covering of his bier, intending to regard such contact as a protection bringing salvation.

14. A certain young girl from the village called Decimae was being carried dead to the tomb; the corpse had already been laid in a wooden coffin, but the chest itself was not yet covered. When those who were carrying her out heard the voices of those singing psalms and escorting the holy body of the blessed bishop, they asked with tears that the bier they were carrying might be drawn over the girl's body. Those [bearers], fired with the ardour of faith and not doubting the outcome, thought their holy prayers should by no means be rejected. And while what they had asked was being done, the people said to one another that the apostolic man, blessed Maximus, whom divine grace had never failed, though he had already paid the debt of nature, nevertheless lived on in miracles and merits. So all together, with the most faithful devotion of heart, they prostrated themselves and prayed at length, and then, rising, when they had cried *Kyrie eleison* seven times, they saw the girl restored to life. For this reason a great terror seized them, and they were filled with amazement mingled with joy. The girl, leaving her funeral clothes and dressed in others, joined the throngs of the crowded people and with a public voice bore witness to her deliverance in praise of the holy bishop in these words: 'O most blessed merits of the bishop! O blessed man, and blessed life of the pontiff, who, to declare that he lives for ever by divine reward, after death raised a dead girl!'

15. At length the body of the most blessed bishop was brought into the town of Riez and, with great ceremony, buried in the church of blessed Peter, which he himself had founded, and which was afterwards called by his name because of his frequent patronage; there whatever is asked with faith is obtained with Christ's help. So let faith not be doubtful, since the power is infinite. Not long after, when many things were being related by many people in commemoration of the holy man, Cariatto the subdeacon, a man of most holy life, publicly testified as follows: 'Let none of us doubt,' he said, 'that the most blessed Maximus, of whose miracles so many things are reported at the prompting of truth, while he lived in the mortal body, conversed no less with angels than with men. For him whom the human condition kept with us, the worth of his merits showed to be a constant companion of the blessed spirits. One night, when the most celebrated feast of blessed Andrew was at hand, and I had been appointed to wake [the others] for the vigils, and in the first part of the night a pleasant sleep had overcome me, anxious though I was, I heard sweet melodies of people singing psalms; and soon, roused, I leapt from my bed in great agitation, thinking I had missed the proper time for waking [them]. Then indeed I drank in with my ears melodies of spiritual songs far sweeter even than could be produced by human efforts. So at once I went with cautious step to the very entrance of the sanctuary, and there I, a sinner, heard the most blessed apostles Peter and Andrew yielding precedence to each other in turn for the honour of completing that prayer with holy Maximus. And when at last blessed Maximus, compelled by continual pressing, could no longer put them off, he completed the office with these words: "Blessed be the glory of God for ever and for ages of ages"; and the rest answered, "Amen." But I, coming closer in my eagerness to find out, could see no one there except the most holy Maximus, lying prostrate, face and body down, on the floor of the church. He, however, rising, rebuked my curiosity, unworthy sinner that I am, with these words: "It is hard for human frailty to know the secrets of the saints, and rash to wish to pry into them; so hear what I, knowing beforehand, am now about to tell you: take care not to make known what you have seen and heard. For on whatever day you do so, you will depart from this light." Whether that is now to happen depends on God's judgement. I, for my part, leave to posterity the memory and testimony of his surpassing power, so that no mortal may be unaware how just men can enjoy the fellowship and company of the saints.' Abundant credence was given to this account by the fact that on that same day the subdeacon, just as had been foretold to him by blessed Maximus, ceased to be among the living; and since he could not prolong the term of his life, neither did he wish to conceal the mystery.

16. Let us therefore, with all devotion and the utmost eagerness of heart, ask almighty God that, relying on the patronage of this most blessed prelate, he may grant us pardon for our sins, and that he for whom we celebrate the present office may always keep our soul pure from deadly vices; and in performing it let us so show ourselves in bodily presence that our minds may shine with the light of charity, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.
